title: Announcing PARG — a language-independent grammar language with bindings on every runtime
summary: PARG is parsanol's grammar language: write one text file, compile it once into a checksummed artifact, and bind its captures to typed model objects — with runtime and compiled object bindings on every runtime: Ruby, Rust, WebAssembly, and TypeScript.

content.text: PARG is parsanol's grammar language, and it is now the recommended way to teach parsanol a new format. One `.parg` text file — rules in an ABNF-flavored style, entry points, bindings, and in-file tests — compiles **once** into a checksummed `parsanol-tree/v2` artifact that Ruby, Rust, WebAssembly, and TypeScript all load, verify, and parse **byte-identically**.
One grammar, every runtime

The compiler lints the grammar — shadowed alternatives and order-dependence are build failures, not runtime surprises — rewrites direct left recursion into left-folding precedence tiers, and runs every in-file test before anything ships. What ships is **data, not code**: a portable grammar envelope with a sha256 checksum over its canonicalized content, and the original source riding inside so any runtime can rebuild it.
Bindings, language-independent
This is what PARG exists for: captures bind to typed model objects on every runtime, without rewriting the grammar per language.

require "parsanol"

document = Parsanol::PARG::Parser.new(File.read("demo.parg")).parse
result   = Parsanol::PARG::Compiler.compile(document)
File.write("demo.artifact.json", JSON.generate(result.envelope))

artifact = Parsanol::PARG::Artifact.load("demo.artifact.json")
artifact.parse_and_bind("identifier", "iso 12345")
# => { publisher: "iso", number: 12345 }

A capture declared with `as` maps to a model field — `string`, `integer`, `float`, or `boolean`, with cardinalities `1`, `0..1`, `1..*`, and `0..*` — plus declarative preprocess steps (`table_lookup`) and data-driven alternatives (`alt from_table`). The same artifact carries runtime and compiled object bindings on every surface parsanol runs on:

rows: The browser — this site's playground runs it

content.text: Every engine verifies the checksum, applies the same bindings, and returns the same tree — that identity is enforced by a 32-artifact conformance corpus and a nightly five-engine differential fuzz, not promised.
What the language has

items: **Skip and trivia injection** — whitespace and comments consumed by declaration, with `capture: comments` so captured trivia becomes data; `atomic` rules opt out for token-shaped bodies.
**Direct left recursion** — `expr = expr "*" expr / INT` is rewritten at compile time into left-folding precedence tiers, identical on every engine.
**Behind-guards** — `!<x` and `&<x` inspect the text behind the position without consuming, for intraword constraints like constrained emphasis.
**Declared recovery** — `resync` policies bake deterministic skip spans into the artifact, so a failed parse reports the deepest position, the partial tree, and the exact spans consumed to resume.
**In-file tests** — `accept` / `reject` / `capture` / `example` / `shape` assertions run at compile time and travel with the artifact, so every runtime replays the same expectations.
**Imports** — existing ABNF, EBNF, and pest grammars come in as PARG text through `Parsanol::PARG::Import`.

content.text: Where to start

items: [What is PARG?](/parg) — the grammar language and the artifact guarantees.
[The language tour](/parg/language) — the whole syntax on one page, with examples.
[The playground](/playground) — parse with the shipped wasm binary in your browser, including the error-recovery grammar with a declared `resync` policy.

content.text: Grammars that use runtime state atoms (`state`, `set`, `switch`, or custom Ruby classes) remain Ruby-tier by contract: the Rust and wasm engines reject such artifacts loudly at the boundary instead of mis-parsing them. Everything else in this post runs identically on all five engines.

title: Error Recovery Everywhere, and a Fifth Engine to Keep It Honest
summary: The recovery stack is complete on every runtime — deepest-failure diagnostics, partial trees, and declared resync spans with byte-identical offsets — verified daily by a five-engine differential fuzz that now includes a reference walker with every optimization switched off.

content.text: Parsanol's recovery stack is finished and shipped on **all five runtimes** — the Ruby interpreter and VM, the Rust packrat walker and its bytecode VM, the wasm build, and the TypeScript runtime:

items: **Deepest-failure diagnostics (F7)** — every failure reports the deepest real-content position with the expected set and ranked alternatives, not the outermost construct.
**Partial trees (R1.5)** — a failed parse still returns the deepest clean prefix, shaped exactly as the root rule would have shaped it.

**Declared resync (R2)** — `resync document = 1*( %x00-3A / %x3C-FF ) ";"` bakes a deterministic skip policy into the artifact: at a failure point the engine consumes each pattern match as one annotated span (`offset → resumed_at`) and resumes parsing. No trial scanning, no heuristics — the author owns the spans, and every engine returns them byte-identically.

content.text: A fifth engine keeps it honest

The nightly differential fuzz grew a fifth path: a **reference walker** with every memo table, fused scan, and fast path switched off — the plain recursive relation the normative semantics document states, nothing more. The whole conformance corpus (32 artifacts, 125 cases) replays identically through it, and an archived one-shot validator — an independent implementation of the semantics written from the document — agrees on **304/304** cases. Two spec ambiguities that run surfaced were fixed in the document, not papered over.
Try it

The [playground](/playground) now ships an error-recovery grammar: break the input and the engine shows the strict failure, the partial tree, and the exact resync span side by side — produced by the same `@parsanol/wasm` binary the conformance suites validate.
**Released:** parsanol-rs 0.18.18 (+ @parsanol/wasm 0.18.18), parsanol (TS) 0.10.13, parsanol-ruby 1.3.107 — all shipped, audited, and replay-verified across the corpus.

title: Parsanol 1.3.52: The Ruby and Rust Packages Ship Together
summary: The Ruby gem and the Rust crate now expose one engine across every supported runtime. This post enumerates the supported formats, archives, runtimes, and platforms.

content.text: Parsanol 1.3.52 marks the first release in which the Ruby gem (`parsanol`) and the Rust crate (`parsanol`) ship from the same build matrix. The two artifacts share a single native engine, expose the same C ABI to non-MRI runtimes, and bundle a vendored copy of one another for the cases in which only one of the two is available.
Two packages, one engine

The Ruby gem at version 1.3.52 (`gem install parsanol`) ships as one source gem plus eleven prebuilt platform gems. The Rust crate at version 0.8.8 (`cargo add parsanol`) compiles the same engine from source. Both packages expose the same set of primitives at the same level of capability: PEG grammars, named captures, scopes, dynamic dispatch, transformations, error reporting, and incremental reparsing.
Supported grammar formats
The engine consumes and produces grammars in the following formats.
The engine accepts any of these as input and produces a parslet-compatible tree from any of them on output.
Supported input archives
The engine parses the following input formats in the standard DSL.

items: Plain text (UTF-8, ASCII, binary-safe via the explicit-length C entry point `parsanol_c_parse_len`)
RFC 3339 date and time values
ISO 8601 date and time values
JSON, XML, CSV, YAML through the corresponding parser libraries
CommonMark markdown
ABNF, RFC 5234 core ABNF
Custom formats defined by the user through the Parsanol DSL

content.text: Supported output archives
The engine emits the following output formats.

items: Parslet-compatible tree (`Hash`, `Array`, `Parsanol::Slice`)
Raw tagged tree (`Parsanol::Native.parse_raw`)
Batch-encoded u64 array for high-throughput consumers (`Parsanol::Native.parse_batch`)
Prefix-parse result (value, end position) (`Parsanol::Native.parse_prefix`)
Raw tagged tree with the `parsanol_c_*` C ABI

content.text: Supported runtimes
The engine runs on the following runtimes.
The FFI tier depends on the `ffi` Ruby gem. MRI users receive the FFI tier as a resilience fallback when the extension fails to load. TruffleRuby users receive the FFI tier as the default engine.
Supported platforms
Each platform gem carries the Ruby extension and a vendored cdylib. The ruby source gem carries no binaries.
The 32-bit x86 Linux target is not shippable: rb-sys does not publish i686 dock images and rake-compiler ships no prebuilt i686 rubies for the 3.2 floor.
How to use each package
Ruby gem
gem install parsanol

The gem installs one source gem plus one prebuilt platform gem per runtime. The MRI extension loads by default. TruffleRuby resolves the host-triple platform gem and loads the FFI tier. JRuby resolves the source gem and runs the pure-Ruby engine.
Rust crate
cargo add parsanol
The crate compiles from source. The `ruby` feature pulls in magnus for the Ruby extension. Without the feature, the crate compiles as a pure portable core that links into any cdylib.
C ABI (ffi tier)

The C ABI is exported by both the MRI extension and the cdylib. The entry points are `parsanol_c_register`, `parsanol_c_parse`, `parsanol_c_parse_len`, `parsanol_c_last_error`, and `parsanol_c_release`. Consumers other than Ruby (Python, Node, Lua) bind these directly.
Release cadence

The Ruby gem and the Rust crate release from the same commit and share the same version floor for major releases. The minor and patch versions advance independently. The Ruby gem leads on release tooling; the Rust crate leads on engine features. The Ruby 1.3.52 release and the Rust 0.8.8 release coincide.

title: 1.3.52: A Vendored C Library in Every Platform Gem
summary: Each prebuilt platform gem now carries its own pure-portable cdylib next to the extension — the ffi tier works everywhere from MRI fallback to TruffleRuby — while the source gem stays binary-free.

content.text: Every prebuilt `parsanol` platform gem for 1.3.52 ships two native artifacts: the Ruby extension and a **pure-portable cdylib** (`libparsanol.{so,dylib}` / `parsanol.dll`) at `lib/parsanol/native/`.
Why a cdylib next to the extension?
The cdylib speaks a plain C ABI with zero Ruby-version coupling — no magnus, no rb-sys. That makes it useful to runtimes that can't load C-API extensions:

items: **TruffleRuby** resolves its host-triple platform gem and gets native parsing through the ffi tier
**MRI** gets a resilience fallback: if the extension ever fails to load on an exotic libc, the ffi tier picks up the cdylib instead of dropping to pure Ruby
The **ruby source gem stays binary-free** — binaries live only in per-platform gems, never in git

content.text: The platform matrix
32-bit x86 Linux is not shippable today: rb-sys stopped publishing i686 dock images and rake-compiler ships no prebuilt i686 rubies for the 3.2+ floor.

Also in this release: binary-safe `parsanol_c_parse_len` on the C ABI (interior NULs survive the boundary), and bounded caches — the compiled-program cache is an LRU, closing the unbounded memory growth reported on dynamic-fragment grammars.

title: Exact Tree Parity: CanFlatten, Dynamic Capture Writes, TreeDiff
summary: Both engines now produce byte-identical parslet trees — the CanFlatten fold is ported exactly, dynamic blocks can read AND write captures across the FFI boundary, and TreeDiff.why explains any divergence in one call.

content.text: Parsanol's compatibility bar moved from "parslet-like" to **exact**: the transformer is now a line-for-line port of Parslet's `CanFlatten` fold (merge_fold, flatten_repetition, named-empty-list semantics), and a differential suite pins Ruby vs Rust vs parslet on shared corpora — including the subtle bare-repeated-sibling-capture cases that historically lost data (#36, #83).
The dynamic bridge, completed
Coradoc-style dispatch grammars — mutually recursive rules keyed on captures — now work natively end to end:

items: blocks **read** `ctx.captures` (capture subtrees travel with the state, content-fingerprinted)
blocks **write** `ctx.captures[:k] = v`, and writes propagate back into the enclosing capture scope with rollback on failed branches
deterministic blocks are pure cache functions of `(input, pos, captures)` — hits replay grammar and writes without re-entering the host

content.text: When trees differ anyway
`Parsanol::TreeDiff.why(a, b)` reports the first divergence with a path — the debugging tool we used to chase the remaining edge cases ourselves.

title: Engine Modernization: Bytecode VM, SIMD Scanning, Incremental Reparse
summary: parsanol-rs 0.6–0.8 ships a bytecode VM with lead-byte dispatch and selective rule memoization, SIMD scan kernels, compiled-program artifact caching, and tree-sitter-style incremental parsing sessions.

content.text: The Rust engine grew three major subsystems across 0.6 → 0.8:
Bytecode VM (`Backend::Bytecode`)
Grammars compile to a flat instruction program with interleaved ordered choice, kinded backtrack frames, and a value model that builds parslet-shaped trees directly. Highlights:

items: **BYTE_DISPATCH**: alternatives with provably disjoint lead-byte sets compile to a single table jump (the KV benchmark parses 47.5 KB in ~3 ms)
**Selective rule memoization**: a CFG dataflow over the compiled program memoizes only rules that never cross host calls or capture writes — sound by construction, no memory tax on dynamic grammars
**Compile-once**: `Parser::with_program` plus an on-disk artifact cache (XDG, versioned format) amortizes compilation across processes

content.text: SIMD scan kernels
Identifier/delimiter classification runs 16/32-byte block membership kernels (NEON always; AVX2 behind runtime detection): ~6.2× on identifier runs, stable under load where scalar collapses.
Incremental reparse

`Parsanol::IncrementalSession` (and `mode: :incremental`) reparse only the dirty span: per-edit tree equality against full reparse is CI-gated, and measured keystroke latency on ~600 KB documents is ~1.5–1.7× better than reparse. Retention is sound across edits — failure entries are never retained, and pool-backed values are re-walked instead of adopted.

title: Parsanol 1.3: The Native-First Era
summary: Native Rust parsing is now the default on every mode — cause-tree errors, prefix and reporter parsing, incremental sessions — with a pure-Ruby engine always underneath as the portable floor.

content.text: Parsanol 1.3 reorganized the gem around one principle: the Rust engine is the default, and every parsing mode runs natively — no silent re-entry into Ruby mid-parse.
What runs natively now

rows: parslet-compatible failure trees built in Rust; no reporter reparse
one `err_at` from the native cause on failure
edit-span reparse with snapshot-tier memo retention

content.text: Grammars that cannot be serialized to Rust (Cut, Infix, custom atoms) fail fast at registration with `Parsanol::Native::UnsupportedGrammar` and route to the Ruby engine — loudly, never silently diverging.
Measured against parslet
Interleaved A/B on real corpora (shared machines, GC-isolated):

items: molecule grammar: native **10.7–12.2×** parslet, ruby **1.7–1.9×**
pubid-ISO corpus: native **6.9×** parslet
asciichem mixed valid/invalid: native **~2.9×** parslet after the native failure path landed

content.text: Memory that stays bounded

Large-input memoization recycles packrat caches at capacity instead of freezing them (expressir's 605 KB giants: 99.8 → 11.5 ms/KB), and a bounded-RSS spec now guards release CI: dozens of distinct documents and repeated parses of one document must not grow RSS.

title: Parsanol 0.4.0: Unified API and Lazy Line/Column
summary: Single parse() API, zero-overhead position info, Ruby 4.0 support, and WASM build fixes.

content.text: Parsanol 0.4.0 simplified the surface and removed the last eager costs from position tracking.
Unified `parse()` API
The specialized entry points collapsed into one:

items: `parse_with_transform(g, i, cache)` → `parse(g, i, map)`
raw atoms keep `parse_with_grammar(atom, i)`

content.text: Lazy line/column
`Slice` carries `offset` and `content`; `line_and_column` is computed on demand and cached after first access — position info costs nothing unless you read it:
result[:name].line_and_column # => [1, 7]
Also in this release

items: Ruby 4.0 support in the extension matrix
WASM build fixes (the wasm target stays behind its feature flag)

title: Parsanol Ruby 1.2.2: FFI Captures, Scopes, and Dynamic Atoms
summary: Ruby bindings now support native capture extraction, isolated scopes, and context-sensitive parsing via FFI callbacks.

content.text: Parsanol Ruby 1.2.2 brings full FFI support for the new features introduced in parsanol-rs 0.3.0. Ruby code can now use capture atoms, scope atoms, and dynamic atoms with native performance.
Version Sync
Capture Atoms in Ruby

require 'parsanol'

parser = str('hello').capture(:greeting)
result = parser.parse('hello world')
puts result[:greeting].to_s  # => "hello"
Dynamic Atoms with Ruby Callbacks

# Type-driven parsing with FFI callbacks
parser = match('[a-z]+').capture(:type) >> str(':') >>
        dynamic { |ctx|
          case ctx[:type].to_s
          when 'int' then match('\d+')
          when 'str' then match('[a-z]+')
          else match('[a-z]+')
          end
        }

result = parser.parse('int:42')
puts result[:type].to_s  # => "int"
Streaming Builder API
The StreamingBuilder module provides maximum performance by eliminating intermediate AST construction. Include `Parsanol::BuilderCallbacks` in your class to receive parse events directly.
What's Changed

items: FFI bindings for capture, scope, and dynamic atoms
`Parsanol::BuilderCallbacks` module for streaming parsing
`Parsanol::Native::Dynamic` module for callback registration
Fixed native extension loading for precompiled gems
1178 tests passing

title: Parsanol 0.3.0: Captures, Scopes, and Dynamic Atoms
summary: Major release adding capture extraction, isolated scopes, and context-sensitive parsing.

content.text: Parsanol 0.3.0 introduces three powerful new features for extracting and managing parsed data: **Capture Atoms**, **Scope Atoms**, and **Dynamic Atoms**.
Capture Atoms
Extract named values from your input, like named groups in regular expressions but integrated into the parsing grammar.
Scope Atoms
Create isolated capture contexts for nested parsing. Captures made inside a scope are discarded when the scope exits.
Dynamic Atoms
Runtime-determined parsing via callbacks. Enable context-sensitive parsing.
Backend Compatibility
What's Changed

items: New `Atom::Capture`, `Atom::Scope`, `Atom::Dynamic` variants
New `ParseResult` methods: `capture_names()`, `get_capture()`, `captures()`
`CaptureState` for zero-copy string storage
Thread-safe dynamic callback registry
Streaming parser capture persistence across chunks
DSL helpers: `capture()`, `scope()`, `dynamic_with_id()`
400+ tests (up from 396)

title: Parsanol Ruby 1.1.0: Slice Support and Performance
summary: Added Slice objects for lazy extraction and streaming parser support for large files.

content.text: Parsanol Ruby 1.1.0 adds Slice objects for lazy extraction and streaming parser support for large files.
Slice Objects
Extract values lazily without loading entire parse results into memory:

require 'parsanol'

parser = str('hello').repeat(1)
result = parser.parse('hellohellohello')

# Access results as Slice objects
result.each_slice do |slice|
  puts slice.to_s  # => "hello"
end
Streaming Parser
Parse large files without loading them entirely into memory:

# Stream parsing for large files
parser = Parsanol::StreamingParser.new(grammar)
parser.parse_file('large_data.json') do |result|
  process(result)
end
Integration Modes Update

title: PARG tree editions: v1 is the default, v2 opts in
summary: PARG grammars can declare `edition "v2"` for fully named parse trees. Edition v1 remains the default; the compiler and loaders validate one edition axis.

content.text: A PARG grammar header can now declare an **edition** — the shape of the tree the compiler bakes into the artifact. `v1` is the default, deliberately: existing grammars keep their capture trees. `v2` is opt-in.

grammar Demo version "1.0.0" { ... }                # v1 — the default
grammar Demo version "1.0.0" edition "v2" { ... }  # v2 — opt-in

`edition` is the canonical spelling; the deprecated `mode` header (a quoted `v1` or `v2` value) remains an alias that canonicalizes to `edition` in the artifact. v2 is a **tree-shape edition, not a syntax edition**: the grammar text is unchanged apart from the header. The compiler wraps every rule reference that produces no capture in `Named(rule_name)`, so consumers read a fully named tree; rules that can only match whitespace ("glue") stay unnamed.

With a literal separator, the same grammar yields `{ k: "abc" }` under v1 and `{ k: "abc", sep: "," }` under v2. Artifacts, checksums, and trees differ, so moving to v2 requires recompiling and redistributing the artifact.

The envelope carries `"edition": "v1" | "v2"`. An unknown edition is rejected instead of parsed with the wrong tree shape: parsanol-ruby 1.3.112 rejects it at compile time and at load, and parsanol-rs 0.19.7 rejects it at load. `parsanol` 1.3.112 or newer is required for `edition` headers.
To see what v2 would name in an existing v1 grammar, run the migration radar with the flag after the file:
bundle exec parsanol parg lint grammars/<flavor>.parg --captures

One open interaction is under review: under v2, a text capture over a rule assembled from lexical references (for example, digits built from a digit rule) arrives as an array of named leaves rather than a string. No reconstruction recipe is documented while the language decision is open.

**Update (2026-10-30):** parsanol 1.3.113 switched the envelope field to integers — `"edition": 1 | 2`. The loaders still read the earlier quoted spellings (`"v1"` / `"v2"`), and artifacts without the field parse as edition 1. The grammar header keeps `edition "v2"`.
